extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of literary theory, aesthetics, and German literature (Schiller/Goethe)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and evaluative principles for judging and producing poetry, drama, and art as presented in a literary-aesthetics textbook (discussion of Schiller, Lessing, Goethe, and German literary history). Emphasizes beauty, the play of faculties, tragic/sublime elements, form vs. matter, and distinctions like simple vs. sentimental poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as active, living unity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus the beautiful is active, living unity, full existence without defect...the idea that is quite present in the appearance, the appearance which is quite formed and penetrated by the idea."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is not a passive property but a fully present idea instantiated in appearance; good art presents the idea so completely in form that the appearance is saturated by it. Anti-pattern: works where appearance and underlying idea remain disconnected or where the idea feels absent from form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as mediator of the divine to the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty...mediates to us in a sensuous sign a heavenly gift of grace, that it opens to us a view into the eternal Being...that it brings the divine even to the perception of sense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong art makes transcendent or moral truths perceptible through sensory form; it should suggest an inner ground (the eternal/godlike) through sensuous representation. Works that are purely decorative without moral or spiritual resonance fail this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's chief aim is giving enjoyment / pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The aim and source of art to consist in giving enjoyment, in pleasing. To nature pleasure is a mediate object, to art its main object."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art by its capacity to provide aesthetic pleasure—suitability and affective response are central. This does not imply triviality; 'pleasure' includes elevation and the sublime. Antipattern: aesthetic theories that deny enjoyment as a criterion for art's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: The play-instinct (free play of faculties) as basis of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiller: man is reason and will (form-instinct) and sensuous being (material-instinct); "in the midst between these two is situated the beautiful...the play instinct"; "Man is only quite a man when he plays."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good art balances form and sensibility, enabling a 'free play' of cognitive and sensuous faculties. Creative work should neither be pure abstraction nor mere sensation but an interplay that yields harmony. Antipatterns: didactic abstraction without feeling; purely sensational work without form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of thought and feeling; form and life united
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty knits together thought and feeling; the fullest unity of spirit and matter...Only inasmuch as life is formed in the understanding and form in feeling does life win a form and form win life, and only thus does beauty arise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work integrates intellectual content and emotional resonance such that neither feels tacked on. Seek works where conceptual rigor and affective immediacy reinforce each other. Antipattern: emotionally manipulative prose lacking conceptual unity; coldly cerebral texts lacking feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness ('das Fassliche') over blind observance of classical unities
rubrics_metrics.description: "The law of the comprehensive--'das Fassliche'--is the principle; and the three unities have only value as far as they attain it...When they become an obstacle to the comprehension it is madness to wish to observe them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (e.g., unity of time/place) are valid only insofar as they serve the work's comprehensibility and expressive power. Prioritize clarity and full exposition of subject matter rather than slavish formal observance. Antipattern: rigid formalism that reduces dramatic or poetic comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs. Sentimental Poetry distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sentimental poetry is the fruit of quiet and retirement; simple poetry the child of life...The sentimental is in danger of extending the limits of human nature too far, of being too ideal, too mystical. Neither character exhausts the ideal of humanity, but the intimate union of both."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poets combine the immediacy of 'simple' poetry (rooted in lived experience) with the reflective depth of 'sentimental' poetry (ideal/moral contemplation). Beware excessive mystification (sentimental) or mere reportage (only simple). Aim for a balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic art and the sublime: suitability and moral adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: On tragic subjects Schiller "applies Kantian principles of the sublime to tragedy...With Kant he shows that the source of all pleasure is suitableness; the touching and sublime elicit this feeling, implying the existence of unsuitableness...the necessity of suffering and the pathetic in connection with moral adaptations to interest us deeply."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragedies by how they employ suffering and the pathetic to evoke the sublime and moral reflection: the emotional impact must be appropriate ('suitable') to the subject and point toward moral significance. Antipattern: gratuitous suffering without moral or philosophical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace and dignity as expression of a beautiful soul
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theme of this paper is the conception of grace, or the expression of a beautiful soul and dignity, or that of a lofty mind...it does full justice to the sensuous and to the moral...an image of perfected humanity in which grace and dignity are united."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary depiction of character should aim to manifest inner moral elevation (dignity) alongside sensuous beauty (grace). Evaluate character portrayal for balance between ethical stature and humane sensibility. Antipattern: characters that are either morally hollow or only decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as moral education and liberation toward the divine
rubrics_metrics.description: "He is a moral educator of his people...Philosophy and poetry are to both a vibration of love in the soul upwards to God, a liberation from the bonds of sense, a purification of man, a moral art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One criterion for great poetry is its capacity to morally elevate readers—to purify, instruct, or open toward higher truths. Assess works for whether they cultivate humanity rather than merely entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic laws within works; freedom paired with responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetical creation was therefore viewed as free, but at the same time responsible...Every work bears in itself the organic laws of its development."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative freedom must be exercised with internal coherence: a work should contain the seeds of its own development (structure, motive, logic). Judge works for internal organicity rather than arbitrary invention. Antipattern: episodic or disjointed works lacking internal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Details of history are its poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "An able critic has said the details which are the truth of history are also its poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical drama/poetry, faithful, vivid detail can be the source of poetic power; accurate and concrete particulars enrich the universal. Evaluate historical works by the authenticity and poetic use of detail. Antipattern: flattening history into abstract sermonizing without concrete texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's task: find the poetry in any subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no subject that has not its poetry; it is for the poet to find it there." (Goethe quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creativity lies partly in perceiving the poetic in ordinary or unexpected subjects. Evaluate originality in the poet's ability to render any subject poetically rather than the subject itself determining value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pomp and affectation in the theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing "sought to banish all pomp from the theatre, and in doing so some critics have thought that he banished the ideal and fell into affectation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical writing should eschew empty grandiosity; strive for truthful expression over pomp. Antipattern: exaggerated mannerisms or artificial grandiosity that obscure genuine sentiment or idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance national/legendary elements with classical forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The second classical period "blend[ed] the national and legendary elements...with the highest effusions of dramatic poetry...in Schiller and Goethe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with national or legendary material, integrate it with disciplined form to achieve expressive maturity. Evaluate how well folklore/legend and formal craft are combined rather than treating them as separate or clashing registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and matter distinction: arrange content but both necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: "By [matter] is implied that which can be determined in general; the [form] implies its determination...That which in the phenomenon corresponds to the sensation, I term its matter; but that which effects that the content...can be arranged under certain relations, I call its form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should attend to both what is represented (matter/content) and how it is organized (form). Good creative work demonstrates mastery of both—rich matter expressed through coherent, appropriate form. Antipattern: excellent ideas ruined by poor form or elegant form empty of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentalism vs realism in ethical/aesthetic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sentimental is in danger of extending the limits of human nature too far...The idealist is a nobler but a far less perfect being; the realist appears far less noble, but is more perfect...the noble lies in the proof of a great capacity, but the perfect in the general attitude of the whole and in the real facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should recognize the trade-off between lofty idealism (nobility) and practical completeness (perfection). Evaluate whether a work's idealism is grounded or slides into implausible sentimentality, and whether realism sacrifices profundity for completeness.
